method: One visual/manual reading per printed page; claims captured as printed, not yet accepted as corrected facts.

facts: The natural-gas production list continues with Western Offshore or KG Basin, Assam, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh.
A separate printed natural-gas production ranking lists Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Assam and Andhra Pradesh.
Uranium is described as pitchblende-derived, radioactive and an electricity-generating nuclear fuel.
India's first uranium mining is dated to 1967 at Jaduguda in Singhbhum district, Jharkhand.
Andhra Pradesh uranium locations listed are Tummalapalle, Rachakuntapalle and Kanampalle in Kadapa and Koppunuru in Guntur.
Jharkhand locations listed are Jaduguda, Bhatin, Narwapahar, Turamdih and Banduhurang in Singhbhum.
Meghalaya uranium is placed in the sandstone belt of Khasi district; Rajasthan uranium is listed at Udaipur and Rohil in Sikar; Telangana uranium at Lambapur-Peddagattu and Chitrial in Nalgonda.
Uranium production is printed for Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand.
Thorium is described as derived from thorite and monazite and as most abundant in India.
Printed thorium resource shares are Andhra Pradesh 31 percent, Tamil Nadu 21 percent and Odisha 20 percent, with Kerala and West Bengal also listed.
Thorium production is listed for Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Odisha.
Titanium is stated to occur mainly in ilmenite; world-leading resources in India are claimed and it is called a metal of the future.
Titanium deposits and production are listed in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Kerala.
Zirconium is placed in zircon-rich Kerala beach sands, with deposits and production listed in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Odisha.
Major minerals are listed as coal, iron, bauxite, copper and manganese, with mica, clay, barytes and feldspar moved from major to minor minerals.
Minor minerals are described as construction stones, gravel, sand, clay and similar materials regulated through state rules.
Seventeen rare-earth metals are said to have economic significance; printed global shares are China 36.7 percent, Brazil 18 percent and India 5.8 percent, placing India fifth.
correction_flags: Natural-gas rankings and rare-earth shares need year-tagged authoritative data.
The claim that India has the world's largest titanium resources needs verification and careful ilmenite-resource wording.
Current district names and mine-status claims require verification.
Major/minor mineral legal classification has changed and must be tied to the relevant statute and date.

facts: China is said to hold about 70 percent of the rare-earth market despite southern India having monazite-bearing coastal sands.
Beryllium, praseodymium and europium are linked with missile guidance or target systems.
Lithium is linked with electric-car batteries and mobile-phone and laptop rechargeable batteries; Bolivia, Chile and Argentina are called the lithium triangle.
Promethium is linked with atomic batteries; scandium with aerospace; gadolinium with cancer treatment; niobium with phones, wireless equipment and Bluetooth.

A 2022 lithium discovery of 5.9 million tonnes is printed for Reasi district, Jammu and Kashmir; exploration is also said to occur in Rajasthan's Nagaur and in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Arunachal Pradesh and Meghalaya.
A yellow table lists ten Indian mineral institutions with headquarters and states.

The table pairs GSI with Kolkata, ONGC with Dehradun, Mineral Exploration Corporation with Nagpur, NMDC and AMD with Hyderabad, Central Fuel Research Institute and Central School of Mining with Dhanbad, Uranium Corporation of India with Jaduguda, Indian Bureau of Mines with Nagpur and Coal India with Kolkata.
The Geological Survey of India is described as headquartered at Kolkata with six regional offices and as established in 1851.
A note says Survey of India was established in 1767 with James Rennell as first Surveyor General, and GSI in 1851.

GSI's stated functions include national mineral-resource scientific information, ground surveys, airborne remote sensing, marine surveys, geoscience, geotechnical and geo-environmental work, glaciology, seismotectonics and natural-hazard studies.
Geological mapping is described as collecting geoscientific data and mapping geological features and structures.
visuals: Yellow three-column table of ten mineral institutions, headquarters and states
correction_flags: Reasi is a GSI inferred lithium resource, not a producing discovery; terminology must be corrected.
Several institutional names are obsolete: MEC is MECL; Central Fuel Research Institute and Indian School of Mines require current names.
Kolkata rather than Calcutta should be used for current headquarters.
Rare-earth applications are simplified and require authoritative technical framing.

facts: A remote-sensing application statement prints a scale of 1:50,000 and mentions multispectral sensors aboard satellites.
The Indian Bureau of Mines is described as a subordinate office of the Ministry of Mines.
IBM functions listed are mineral-resource development, mineral conservation, environmental protection in mines, scientific oversight of mines, coal, petroleum and atomic minerals excluded.
The National Mineral Policy 2019 is stated to replace the 2008 policy after a Supreme Court-appointed committee and Ministry of Mines process.
The policy is described as promoting transparent exploration and allocation while addressing private investment through an exploration corridor or similar mechanism.
A large map titled Coal Fields of India groups coalfields into four categories.
Category I lists Jharia, East Bokaro, Raniganj and North Karanpura.
Category II lists South Karanpura, Rajmahal, Sohagpur and Pench-Kanhan.
Category III lists Pranhita-Godavari Valley, Ib River, Talcher and Wardha Valley.
Category IV lists Cambay Basin, Rajasthan, Northeast India, Jammu and Kashmir and Neyveli.

The map separately numbers Raniganj, Rajmahal, Jharia, East and West Bokaro, North and South Karanpura, Singrauli, Talcher, Ib Valley, Korba-Mand-Raigarh, Sohagpur, Sonhat-Bisrampur, Wardha Valley, Kamptee, Pench-Kanhan-Tawa-Pathakhera, Godavari and Makum coalfields or regions.
visuals: Large Coal Fields of India map with category legend and numbered coalfield key
correction_flags: The map mixes coal rank or importance categories with geological basin categories and must not be reproduced as an authoritative classification without a source.
Institutional jurisdiction and exclusions of IBM require current statutory verification.
The printed remote-sensing sentence is incomplete on this page and needs context.

facts: The Andhra Pradesh mineral-resources section calls the state a mineral storehouse and gemstone or ratnagarbha because of varied metallic and non-metallic minerals.
The state is printed first nationally in mica, barytes, uranium, thorium and titanium resources.
Rajasthan is printed second after Andhra Pradesh in silver, zinc and lead, while Karnataka is printed second in gold, laterite, mica and uranium production.
Hematite iron ore occurrences are listed in Anantapur or Obulapuram, Kadapa or Rachakuntapalle and Nagayalanka, Guntur, Krishna, Kurnool and Nellore districts.
Magnetite iron ore is listed mainly in Prakasam district at Jallikunta and Peddadavalapadu; production is printed only for Visakhapatnam Kadapa Anantapur and Kurnool.
Manganese occurrences are listed in Srikakulam and Vizianagaram areas and production only in Vizianagaram.
Bauxite occurrences are listed in the former Visakhapatnam district at Galikonda, Katuki and Chintapalle, at Sarpavaram in Anakapalle and in East Godavari; no production is printed.

Copper occurrences are listed in Guntur at Agnigundala, Kurnool at Ganikaluva, Gamukonda and Gajulakonda, Kadapa at Jangamarajupalle, Anantapur at Medigubba and Nellore at Masayapeta; production is printed in Guntur and Kurnool.
Zinc occurrences are listed in Guntur, Palnadu or Karamapudi, Prakasam or Markapuram-Mallapuram and Kadapa or Gajulapalle; no production is printed.
Lead occurrences are listed in Kurnool or Chityala-Cheriyu, Palnadu or Karamapudi and Kadapa or Jangamarajupalle; no production is printed.
Chromium occurrences and production are printed only for Krishna district.
Tungsten occurrences are listed in East Godavari and Anantapur, with no production.
Nickel occurrences are listed in Kadapa, with no production.
structured_records: Andhra Pradesh metallic-mineral occurrence and production list
correction_flags: Several locality spellings are uncertain and require IBM or state DMG verification.
Resource and production ranks are date-sensitive and some appear contradictory or unsupported.
District names mix old and new administrative boundaries and must be date-labeled.
Resource occurrence must be distinguished from economically workable reserves and current production.

facts: Gold resources are printed as 47.17 tonnes by GSI, with occurrences in Chittoor, Kurnool and Sri Sathya Sai districts.
Ramgiri, Erragudi and Pagadarayi in the Kurnool district belt are said to have been mined by Deccan Gold Mines Limited with potential annual production of 750 kilograms.
Ramagiri in Sri Sathya Sai and Penakacherla in Anantapur are also linked with exploration by Deccan Gold Mines, and Chigargunta or Chigargunta-type occurrences are mentioned in Chittoor.
Silver occurrences are listed in Guntur and Kurnool, with no production.
Diamond occurrences are listed in Anantapur at Vajrakarur and Kalyandurg, Sri Sathya Sai at Kanganapalle, and Guntur, Bellamkonda, Krishna and Kurnool.

Mica is described as a principal Andhra Pradesh mineral; occurrences include Gudur and Venkatagiri in former Nellore, Atmakur, Podalakur or related Nellore sites, and Krishna or Tiruvuru; production is printed for Tirupati and Nellore.

Limestone occurrences are listed across Anantapur, Kadapa, East and West Godavari, Palnadu, Nandyal and Kurnool; production locations include Betamcherla, Koilkuntla and Dhone in Nandyal, Jammalamadugu and Mydukur in Kadapa, Palnadu and Tummalapenta in Anantapur.
Barytes occurrences are listed in Annamayya, Kadapa, Anantapur, Nellore and Kurnool; production is listed at Mangampeta in Annamayya and in Kadapa, Anantapur and Nellore.
Dolomite production and occurrences are listed for Nandyal, Anantapur and Kadapa.
Marble production and occurrences are listed for Kadapa and Annamayya.
Feldspar production and occurrences are listed for Prakasam and Kadapa.
Granite production and occurrences are printed by grade: Galaxy or A-grade around Prakasam, B-grade around Krishna and Chittoor, and C-grade in other districts.
Asbestos occurrences are listed across several Rayalaseema districts with no production.
structured_records: Andhra Pradesh non-metallic-mineral occurrence and production list
correction_flags: Gold reserve, exploration and proposed-production claims require current GSI and IBM verification.
The Deccan Gold Mines company narrative may conflate prospects and producing mines.
Administrative boundaries and locality spellings require normalization.
Granite A/B/C grade classification is not self-explanatory and needs an authoritative source.

facts: Graphite occurrences are listed in former Visakhapatnam, Eluru and East Godavari districts; production only in East Godavari.
Graphite is stated to be less than 5 percent of national resources and used in pencils, colours and foundry moulds; no current Andhra Pradesh production is printed elsewhere in the same paragraph.
Uranium deposits are described as radioactive and spread in Kadapa and Kurnool districts, with about 70,000 tonnes around Tummalapalle in Kadapa.

Uranium production at Tummalapalle is printed as more than 12 tonnes per month, with additional resource identification over 2,200 hectares; mine work is dated from November 2007 and plant production from 2013.
A second uranium unit is said to be established by the Uranium Corporation at Seripalle or a similarly printed locality.
Uranium mining and exploration around Mylavaram, Khajipeta and Proddatur are attributed to AMD and aerial surveys, with hydrostatic drilling rigs mentioned in Kadapa, Prakasam and Anantapur borders.

Monazite is said to yield thorium and to occur in beach-sand deposits around Bhimunipatnam, Chintapalle and Mukkamala in northern coastal Andhra and also around Konaseema and Nellore; no radioactive mineral production is printed.
Titanium is said to be obtained from ilmenite; deposits and production are printed for Bhavanapadu in Srikakulam and also Konaseema and Nellore.
Petroleum and natural-gas deposits are stated to occur in Krishna-Godavari coastal areas up to about 40,000 square kilometres offshore.

The Ravva basin is linked with Chintalapudi, Pasarlapudi or Pasuvullanka, Bhimunipatnam and other areas; first state petroleum was reportedly found on 19 December 1979 at Lingaboyanacherla near Narsapur in West Godavari.
Apatite occurrences are printed only for former Visakhapatnam, with no production.
Quartz occurrences are listed in Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai, Kadapa, Annamayya, Palnadu and Nellore, with production in Nellore, Sri Sathya Sai, Annamayya and Palnadu.
Calcite occurrences are listed in Alluri Sitarama Raju, Anantapur and Kurnool, with production in Alluri and Anantapur.
Garnet occurrences are listed in Anantapur, Chittoor, Kadapa and Vizianagaram, with production in Anantapur and Chittoor.
structured_records: Apatite, quartz, calcite and garnet occurrence-production list
correction_flags: Graphite production statements appear internally inconsistent.
Uranium tonnage, monthly production, area and dates require UCIL or AMD verification and clear resource versus output units.
The 40,000 square-kilometre KG offshore claim and first-petroleum date require DGH or ONGC verification.
Several place names are unclear and must not be silently normalized.

facts: Zircon occurrences are listed in Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram Manyam, Anakapalle and Kurnool; production in Vizianagaram, Kurnool, Anakapalle, Parvathipuram Manyam and Srikakulam.
Rutile deposits and production are printed only for Srikakulam.
Sillimanite deposits and production are printed only for Srikakulam.
Steatite occurrences are listed in Kurnool, Nandyal and Anantapur; production in Anantapur, Nandyal and Kurnool.
Kyanite deposits are printed only for Nellore, with no production.

Lithium occurrences are listed in Kadapa at Murchintala and in Anantapur at Vankatampalle or a similarly printed locality and Rajupalem; the page says they were discovered in 2024 and no production exists.

A boxed APPSC Group-II 2024 matching PYQ asks to match manganese, barytes, mica and limestone with former Visakhapatnam and East Godavari coastal areas, Garividi in Vizianagaram, Jammalamadugu and Mydukur in Kadapa, and Nellore region.
The printed answer key for the APPSC Group-II 2024 item is option 2: a-II, b-I, c-IV, d-III.
structured_records: Zircon, rutile, sillimanite, steatite, kyanite and lithium occurrence-production list
correction_flags: The 2024 lithium discovery statement requires authoritative confirmation and resource classification.
The PYQ must retain exam identity and be checked against the official key before scoring.
District and locality spellings require authoritative normalization.
